content: 1. Vancomycin Dosing for Clostridium difficile-Associated Diarrhea: Vancomycin is administered orally at a dose of 5–2 g/day, divided every 6–8 hours, for a duration of 7–10 days. This regimen is indicated for the treatment of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea. Firvanq is also approved for this indication. 2. Vancomycin for Infective Endocarditis: Vancomycin is indicated for the treatment of infective endocarditis caused by susceptible isolates of MRSA, viridans group streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus, Enterococcus species, and Corynebacterium species. For enterococcal endocarditis, vancomycin should be used in combination with an aminoglycoside. It is also used in methicillin-susceptible staphylococcal infections in patients allergic to penicillin or those who cannot tolerate or have failed other therapies. For early-onset prosthetic valve endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis, vancomycin is used in combination with rifampin and an aminoglycoside. Dosing considerations vary based on the timing of infection (<1 month or ≥1 month). 3. Vancomycin for Septicemia: Vancomycin is indicated for septicemia caused by susceptible isolates of MRSA, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and methicillin-susceptible staphylococci in penicillin-allergic patients or those who cannot tolerate or have failed other therapies. 4. Vancomycin for Skin and Skin Structure Infections: Vancomycin is used to treat skin and skin structure infections caused by MRSA, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and methicillin-susceptible staphylococci in penicillin-allergic patients or those who cannot tolerate or have failed other therapies. 5. Vancomycin for Bone Infections: Vancomycin is indicated for bone infections caused by MRSA, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and methicillin-susceptible staphylococci in penicillin-allergic patients or those who cannot tolerate or have failed other therapies. 6. Vancomycin for Lower Respiratory Tract Infections: Vancomycin is used to treat lower respiratory tract infections caused by MRSA, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and methicillin-susceptible staphylococci in penicillin-allergic patients or those who cannot tolerate or have failed other therapies. 7. Renal Considerations: Vancomycin is excreted by the kidneys, and patients with impaired renal function are at increased risk of adverse reactions. Elderly patients, who are more likely to have reduced renal function, require careful dose selection and monitoring of renal function during and after treatment to detect potential nephrotoxicity. 8. Drug Interactions: Nephrotoxicity and Ototoxicity: Vancomycin, when used with other nephrotoxic or ototoxic agents (e.g., aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cisplatin, colistin, polymyxin B, and others), increases the risk of these toxicities. Close monitoring or therapy modification is recommended. Live Vaccines: Vancomycin decreases the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines (e.g., BCG, cholera, typhoid) due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is completed. Intestinal Flora Alteration: Vancomycin can reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives, biotin, pyridoxine, and other agents by altering intestinal flora. Caution and monitoring are advised. Renal Clearance: Drugs that decrease renal clearance (e.g., NSAIDs like ibuprofen, aspirin, and ketorolac) can increase vancomycin levels, particularly in neonates. Monitoring is recommended. Methotrexate: Recent vancomycin exposure may impair methotrexate excretion, increasing toxicity risk. Renal function should be assessed, and methotrexate dosing adjusted accordingly. 9. Special Populations: Neonates: Drug interactions that affect vancomycin levels (e.g., NSAIDs) are more pronounced in neonates. Elderly Patients: Elderly patients may take longer to respond to therapy and are at higher risk for nephrotoxicity. Renal function should be closely monitored. 10. Additional Considerations: Vancomycin may increase the levels of certain drugs (e.g., digoxin, peramivir) by altering renal clearance. Co-administration with nephrotoxic agents (e.g., tacrolimus, cyclosporine) requires caution and close monitoring. Vancomycin may decrease the efficacy of sodium picosulfate by altering colonic bacterial flora needed for drug activation.
